In the [[mathematics|mathematical]] discipline of [[graph theory]], the '''expander walk sampling theorem''' intuitively states that [[Sampling (statistics)|sampling]] [[vertex (graph theory)|vertices]] in an [[expander graph]] by doing relatively short [[Random walk#On graphs|random walk]] can simulate sampling the vertices [[statistical independence|independently]] from a [[uniform distribution (discrete)|uniform distribution]].
The earliest version of this theorem is due to {{harvtxt|Ajtai|Komlós|Szemerédi|1987}}, and the more general version is typically attributed to {{harvtxt|Gillman|1998}}.

==Statement==
Let  <math>G=(V,E)</math> be an n-vertex [[expander graph]] with positively weighted edges, and let <math>A\subset V</math>. Let <math>P
</math> denote the [[stochastic matrix]] of the graph, and let <math>\lambda_2</math> be the second largest [[Eigenvalues and eigenvectors|eigenvalue]] of <math display="inline">P</math>. Let <math>y_0, y_1, \ldots, y_{k-1}</math> denote the vertices encountered in a <math>(k-1)</math>-step random walk on <math>G</math> starting at vertex <math>y_0</math>, and let <math display="inline">\pi (A):=</math> <math>\lim_{k\rightarrow\infty} \frac{1}{k} \sum_{i = 0}^{k-1} \mathbf{1}_A(y_i)</math>. Where <math display="inline">\mathbf{1}_A(y)\begin{cases} 1, & \text{if }y \in A \\ 0, & \text{otherwise }\end{cases}</math>

(It is well known<ref>{{Cite book|last=Doob|first=J.L.|title=Stochastic Processes|publisher=Wiley|year=1953|location=Theorem 6.1}}</ref> that almost all trajectories <math>y_0, y_1, \ldots, y_{k-1}</math> converges to some limiting point, <math display="inline">\pi (A)</math>, as <math display="inline">k \rightarrow
</math><math display="inline">\infty

</math>.)

The theorem states that for a weighted graph <math>G=(V,E)</math> and a random walk <math>y_0, y_1, \ldots, y_{k-1}</math> where <math>y_0</math> is chosen by an initial distribution <math display="inline">\mathbf{q}</math>,  for all <math>\gamma > 0</math>, we have the following bound:

:<math>\Pr\left[\bigg| \frac{1}{k} \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} \mathbf{1}_A(y_i) - \pi(A)\bigg| \geq \gamma\right] \leq C e^{-\frac{1}{20} (\gamma^2 (1-\lambda_2) k)}.</math>

Where <math>C</math> is dependent on <math>\mathbf{q}, G </math> and <math>A
</math>.

The theorem gives a bound for the [[rate of convergence]] to <math>\pi(A)</math> with respect to the length of the random walk, hence giving a more efficient method to estimate <math>\pi(A)</math> compared to independent sampling the vertices of <math>G</math>.

==Proof==
In order to prove the theorem, we provide a few definitions followed by three lemmas.

Let <math>\it{w}_{xy}</math> be the weight of the edge <math>xy\in E(G)</math> and let <math display="inline">\it{w}_x=\sum_{y:xy\in E(G)}\it{w}_{xy}.</math> Denote by <math display="inline">\pi(x):=\it{w}_x/\sum_{y\in V} \it{w}_y</math>. Let <math display="inline">\frac{\mathbf{q}}{\sqrt\pi}</math> be the matrix with entries<math display="inline">\frac{\mathbf{q}(x)}{\sqrt{\pi(x)}}</math> , and let <math display="inline">N_{\pi,\mathbf{q}}=||\frac{\mathbf{q}}{\sqrt\pi}||_{2}</math>.

Let <math>D=\text{diag}(1/\it{w}_i )</math> and <math>M=(\it{w}_{ij})</math>. Let <math display="inline">P(r)=PE_r</math> where <math display="inline">P</math> is the stochastic matrix, <math display="inline">E_r=\text{diag}(e^{r\mathbf{1}_A})</math> and <math display="inline">r \ge 0
</math>. Then:
:<math>P = \sqrt{D}S\sqrt{D^{-1}} \qquad \text{and} \qquad P(r) = \sqrt{DE_r^{-1}}S(r)\sqrt{E_rD^{-1}}</math>
Where <math>S:=\sqrt{D}M\sqrt{D} \text{ and } S(r) := \sqrt{DE_r}M\sqrt{DE_r}</math>. As <math>S</math> and <math>S(r)</math> are symmetric, they have real eigenvalues. Therefore, as the eigenvalues of <math>S(r)</math> and <math>P(r)</math> are equal, the eigenvalues of <math display="inline">P(r)</math> are real. Let <math display="inline">\lambda(r)</math> and <math display="inline">\lambda_2(r)</math> be the first and second largest eigenvalue of <math display="inline">P(r)</math> respectively.

For convenience of notation, let <math display="inline">t_k=\frac{1}{k} \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} \mathbf{1}_A(y_i)</math>, <math display="inline">\epsilon=\lambda-\lambda_2
</math>, <math display="inline">\epsilon_r=\lambda(r)-\lambda_2(r)
</math>, and let <math>\mathbf{1}</math> be the all-1 vector.

'''<big>Lemma 1</big>'''

<math>\Pr\left[t_k- \pi(A) \ge \gamma\right] \leq e^{-rk(\pi(A)+\gamma)+k\log\lambda(r)}(\mathbf{q}P(r)^k\mathbf{1})/\lambda(r)^k</math>

'''Proof:'''

By [[Markov's inequality]],

<math>\begin{alignat}{2}
\Pr\left[t_k \ge \pi(A) +\gamma\right] =\Pr[e^{rt_k}\ge e^{rk(\pi(A)+\gamma)}]\leq e^{-rk(\pi(A)+\gamma)}E_\mathbf{q}e^{rt_k}
\end{alignat}</math>

Where <math>E_\mathbf{q}</math> is the expectation of <math>x_0</math> chosen according to the probability distribution <math>\mathbf{q}</math>. As this can be interpreted by summing over all possible trajectories <math>x_0,x_1,.. .,x_k</math>, hence:

<math>E_{\mathbf{q}}e^{rt}=\sum_{x_1,x_2,...,x_k}e^{rt}\mathbb{q}(x_0)\Pi_{i=1}^kp_{x_{i-1}x_i}=\mathbf{q}P(r)^k\mathbf{1}</math>

Combining the two results proves the lemma.

'''<big>Lemma 2</big>'''

For <math> 0\le r \le 1</math>,
:<math>(\mathbf{q}P(r)^k\mathbf{1})/\lambda(r)^k\le (1+r)N_{\pi,\mathbf{q}}</math>
'''Proof:'''

As eigenvalues of <math>P(r)</math> and <math>S(r)</math> are equal,

<math>\begin{align}
(\mathbf{q}P(r)^k\mathbf{1})/\lambda(r)^k&= (\mathbf{q}P\sqrt{DE_r^{-1}}S(r)^k 
\sqrt{D^{-1}E_r}\mathbf{1})/\lambda(r)^k\\ &\le e^{r/2}||\frac{\mathbf{q}}{\sqrt{\pi}}||_2||S(r)^k||_2||\sqrt{\pi}||_2/\lambda(r)^k\\
&\le e^{r/2}N_{\pi,\mathbf{q}}\\
&\le (1+r)N_{\pi,\mathbf{q}}\qquad \square
\end{align}</math>

'''Lemma 3'''

If <math>r</math> is a real number such that <math>0\le e^r-1\le \epsilon/4</math>,
:<math>\log\lambda(r)\le r\pi(A)+5r^2/\epsilon</math>
'''Proof summary:'''

We Taylor expand <math display="inline">\log \lambda(y)
</math> about point <math display="inline">r=z
</math> to get:
:<math>\log\lambda(r)= \log\lambda(z)+m_z(r-z)+(r-z)^2\int_0^1 (1-t)V_{z+(r-z)t}dt</math>
Where <math>m_x \text{ and } V_x</math> are first and second derivatives of <math>\log \lambda(r)</math> at <math>r=x</math>.  We show that <math>m_0=\lim_{k \to \infty}t_k=\pi(A).</math> We then prove that (i) <math display="inline">\epsilon_r\ge 3\epsilon/4</math> by matrix manipulation, and then prove (ii)<math>V_r\le 10/\epsilon</math> using (i) and [[Cauchy's estimate]] from [[complex analysis]].

The results combine to show that 
:<math>\begin{align}
\log\lambda(r)= \log\lambda(0)+m_0r+r^2\int_0^1 (1-t)V_{rt}dt
\le r\pi(A)+5r^2/\epsilon
\end{align}</math>
:A line to line proof can be found in Gilman (1998)[https://epubs.siam.org/doi/pdf/10.1137/S0097539794268765#page23]
'''Proof of theorem'''

Combining lemma 2 and lemma 3, we get that
:<math>\Pr[t_k-\pi(A)\ge \gamma]\le(1+r)N_{\pi,\mathbf{q}}e^{-k(r\gamma-5r^2/\epsilon)}</math>
Interpreting the exponent on the right hand side of the inequality as a quadratic in <math>r</math> and minimising the expression, we see that 
:<math>\Pr[t_k-\pi(A)\ge \gamma]\le(1+\gamma\epsilon/10)N_{\pi,\mathbf{q}}e^{-k\gamma^2\epsilon/20}</math>
A similar bound
:<math>\Pr[t_k-\pi(A)\le - \gamma]\le (1+\gamma\epsilon/10)N_{\pi,\mathbf{q}}e^{-k\gamma^2\epsilon/20}</math>
holds, hence setting <math>C=2(1+\gamma\epsilon/10)N_{\pi,\mathbf{q}}</math> gives the desired result.

==Uses==
This theorem is useful in randomness reductions in the study of [[derandomization]],<ref>{{cite arXiv | eprint=2501.07752 | last1=Anand | first1=Emile | title=Towards the Pseudorandomness of Expander Random Walks for Read-Once ACC0 circuits | date=2025 | class=cs.CC }}</ref> showing that expander random walks are good pseudorandom generators against various classes of test functions. Sampling from an expander walk is an example of a randomness-efficient [[sample (statistics)|sampler]].  Note that the number of [[bit]]s used in sampling <math>k</math> independent samples from <math>f</math> is <math>k \log n</math>, whereas if we sample from an infinite family of constant-degree expanders this costs only <math>\log n + O(k)</math>.  Such families exist and are efficiently constructible, e.g. the [[Ramanujan graph]]s of [[Alexander Lubotzky|Lubotzky]]-Phillips-[[Peter Sarnak|Sarnak]].
